title: Roland Barthes
tradition: Poststructuralism: semiology and writing the self
summary: Roland Barthes began as a student of signs: he showed how mass culture passes off its conventions as "nature" — he called this "myth." Later he came to a very personal kind of writing — about love, pleasure, photography and grief for his mother. Barthes teaches us to see which borrowed scripts we are living out, and to carefully keep what belongs to us alone.
onEmotions: For Barthes, feelings are always partly spoken in ready-made language: we love, feel jealous and pine according to patterns taken from novels, songs and advertising. But he doesn't debunk feelings as "not real." In A Lover's Discourse he describes them as "figures" — recognizable little scenes that everyone lives through — and in doing so gives them back their dignity. In his late books he defends what cannot be reduced to any code: the "punctum," the detail that wounds you in particular, and a grief that refuses to be called "mourning." Barthes proposes a double movement: notice the borrowed script — and keep what is your own, singular.

anxiety.text: The phone is silent, and imagination is already painting the worst: in A Lover's Discourse Barthes calls such little scenes "figures" — recurring gestures of the soul in which we recognize ourselves. The anxiety running ahead of you now, living through a catastrophe that hasn't happened, is one of these figures, and it is exhausting. Drawing on the psychoanalyst Winnicott, Barthes notes that a lover's anxiety is the fear of a loss that has perhaps already happened, long ago, in the past. That is, anxiety often speaks not of tomorrow but of an old wound. Barthes doesn't "treat" anxiety; he describes it — and there is relief in that: your experience has a form, others have lived in it before, it doesn't make you "wrong." To name the figure is to step back from it a little and see a script, not a verdict.
anxiety.practice: Tell yourself your anxiety under your breath, as a scene from a novel, in the third person: "She is waiting, and it seems to her that…" Notice how the scene moves a little further off.

fear.text: "The only passion of my life has been fear" — Barthes set these words of Hobbes as the epigraph to The Pleasure of the Text. Fear can be very bodily and ancient, and Barthes treated it without shame. The epigraph is not a confession of cowardice but honesty: fear accompanies anyone who lives attentively. In Mythologies Barthes showed how culture supplies us with ready-made images of threat and rescue. So Barthes would probably suggest asking: what part of my fear is my own, and what came from other people's plots — the news, advertising, family stories? Separating them doesn't cancel the fear. But your own fear, separated from the "myth," usually turns out smaller, more concrete and more bearable.
fear.practice: Imagine your fear as a frame from a film and ask: where have I seen this picture before — in my own life, or in the news, advertising, family stories? Separate the "myth" from what is yours.

sadness.text: A strap on a shoe in an old family photograph — and suddenly a prick that nothing explains: Barthes called such a detail the "punctum." Sadness, too, often arrives unannounced — from a song, a smell, someone's gesture — and doesn't have to explain itself. In Camera Lucida he distinguishes two ways of looking. The "studium" is a calm, general interest: we understand what is shown and assess it. The "punctum" (from the Latin for "prick") is a chance detail that suddenly wounds you in particular: someone's hands, a shoe strap, the expression of the eyes. The punctum can't be predicted and can't be handed on to someone else. Sadness is often built like a punctum too: it catches on a small thing because that small thing holds what is dear to you. It's enough to acknowledge: this touched me — so it matters to me.
sadness.practice: Find the "prick" of your sadness — the specific detail it started with. Name it to yourself without explanation and simply stay with it for a minute.

grief.text: For almost two years after his mother's death in 1977, Barthes wrote down his states on index cards; later these notes were published as Mourning Diary. Grief is not a problem to be solved but a form of love for someone who is no longer here. Barthes resisted ready-made words: the notion of "mourning," with its stages and "grief work," seemed to him too general, turning living pain into a process that is supposed to "pass" on schedule. He noticed that his sorrow didn't diminish evenly but came in waves. In Camera Lucida he goes through photographs of his mother and truly recognizes her only in one picture, where she is a child — the "Winter Garden" photograph. Barthes grants the right to grieve in your own way, without a timetable, and reminds us: small, precise words about your loss are worth more than any general ones.
grief.practice: Write one short sentence about your loss on a card — not a general one, but a precise one, as Barthes did. Just one for today.

quote.text: Not say mourning. It's too psychoanalytic. I'm not mourning. I'm suffering.
quote.author: Roland Barthes

loneliness.text: "The language of love today is extremely solitary" — with this admission Barthes opens A Lover's Discourse. Loneliness hurts partly because it seems that only you feel this way. Perhaps thousands of people speak the language of love, but no one supports it — serious scholarship ignores it, fashion mocks it as "sentimental." And Barthes decides to let this voice speak. His book is made of "figures" — recognizable moments that each person has lived through alone: waiting, jealousy, the feeling of "I'm not needed." The paradox is that the most private experience turns out to be shared: many have lived it, only in silence. For Barthes, loneliness can be not only endured but also heard as speech that lacks a listener — and sometimes that listener becomes a book, a letter, a note.
loneliness.practice: Open a book you love and find a sentence that sounds as if it were said about your loneliness. Read it aloud: this speech has found a listener.

quote.text: The lover's discourse is today of an extreme solitude.
quote.author: Roland Barthes

anger.text: Two people quarrel, and each wants the last word — in A Lover's Discourse Barthes calls this figure "Scene." Anger is a signal that something important to you has been touched, and Barthes closely observed how it turns into language. Barthes notes that a scene almost never resolves the dispute; it is driven by the desire to win in speech. In his lectures on "the Neutral" he looked for ways out of such rigid confrontations where there must be a winner and a loser. For Barthes, anger doesn't need to be suppressed — you can refuse the fight for the last word: acknowledge your feeling but not turn it into an endless duel. Then the anger stays yours, instead of steering you.
anger.practice: In your next argument, let yourself not have the last word: pause, breathe out, and say one sentence about what you actually want the other person to understand.

shame.text: Which body is beautiful, which life is successful — in Mythologies Barthes showed how culture turns such agreements into "nature," and he called this "myth." The shame that makes you want to vanish and hide from others' eyes doesn't mean something is wrong with you. Then part of shame is not your "defect" but a collision with a myth that passes itself off as nature. In the Fragments Barthes also writes about the "obscenity" of love: today what's awkward is not the explicit but the sentimental, and the lover is most ashamed of their tenderness. Barthes doesn't feel ashamed along with them — he defends the right to "ridiculous" feelings. And he suggests a question: who decided this is shameful?
shame.practice: Imagine that the rule you supposedly broke is printed in a glossy magazine as something "natural." Ask: is this nature or someone's agreement — and who signed it?

guilt.text: Being late, looking at someone the wrong way, seeming tired — A Lover's Discourse has a figure called "Faults," in which the lover feels guilty over trifles, and the petty guilt swells because behind it stands an enormous concern for the other. The guilt you feel shows that you care how your actions affect others. Barthes shows this mechanism without mockery: here guilt is a by-product of attachment. Barthes would probably advise distinguishing a real mistake, which can be admitted and corrected, from the "figure" of guilt that spins on its own and feeds on anxious love. The first can be named and let go. The second can be seen as a sign of your attachment, not as proof that you're a bad person.
guilt.practice: Put a hand on your chest and say two sentences to yourself: "This is what I actually did…" and "This is what I'm imagining…". Feel how differently they sound in your body.

envy.text: We often begin to desire someone simply because others have shown us that they are desirable — Barthes calls this figure "Induction." Envy is unpleasant and often embarrassing, but it simply shows what you want. Desire is contagious; it is passed on through someone else's gaze. And in Mythologies Barthes analyzed how magazines and advertising turn a certain way of life into a standard, as if it were a natural norm. So envy is partly the effect of someone else pointing, not a measure of your failure. That doesn't make it fake. But if you ask who taught you to want exactly this, you can separate a borrowed desire from your own — and your own will turn out quieter, but truer.
envy.practice: Walk down a street — or through a feed — and notice who or what is "showing" you what to desire right now: a shop window, an ad, someone's gaze. Then ask what part of the desired thing is truly yours.

emptiness.text: At the very center of Tokyo, Barthes wrote in Empire of Signs, there is an emptiness: the closed imperial palace, invisible to the city's residents, and the huge city revolves around this empty place without becoming meaningless. Emptiness and apathy are frightening — it seems there's nothing inside and it will always be this way — and this is a real state that deserves gentleness, not reproach. A haiku, for Barthes, interprets nothing and teaches nothing — it simply points: "like this." Emptiness can be a pause in the endless production of meanings, a rest from constant explanation. It doesn't need to be filled immediately. Sometimes it's enough to notice something simple — a light, a sound, a taste — without conclusion or moral.
emptiness.practice: Look out the window and find one thing about which you can only say "like this": light on a wall, a branch, a bird. Look at it for a minute without interpreting anything.

confusion.text: "The birth of the reader must be at the cost of the death of the Author" — so ends Barthes's famous essay. Confusion arises when familiar explanations stop working and there is no single right answer. In "The Death of the Author" Barthes argued that a text's meaning isn't hidden in the head of the author, who alone knows the "correct" interpretation. A text is a tissue of quotations, and it comes together in the reader. The same is probably true of life: we are surrounded by contradictory voices — parents, books, culture — and none of them owns the final truth about you. Then confusion is not a malfunction but the moment when you stop being the performer of someone else's script and become the reader of your own life. You don't have to rush toward a "final" meaning; several interpretations can live side by side.
confusion.practice: Read aloud two or three opposing interpretations of your situation, the way you would read quotations from different books. Don't pick any — let them sound side by side, like a "tissue of quotations."

quote.text: The birth of the reader must be at the cost of the death of the Author.
quote.author: Roland Barthes

fatigue.text: In his lecture course The Neutral (1978), Barthes devoted a separate fragment to fatigue — and spoke of it with respect. Your tiredness is not laziness or defeat but an honest signal from body and soul. Barthes saw in it not only exhaustion but also a quiet refusal of the constant need to take a position, argue, choose a side, "produce" opinions. The "Neutral" for Barthes is not indifference but a desire to step out of an imposed confrontation, the right not to answer every challenge. Then tiredness can be understood as a legitimate demand for a pause, not as a personal defect. The world expects continuous clarity and activity from you. Barthes reminds us: you can for a while have no opinion, not decide, not choose — and there is dignity in that too.
fatigue.practice: Choose one topic for today on which you allow yourself to have no opinion. Notice how this small freedom feels.

boredom.text: Bliss seen from the shores of pleasure — this is how Barthes defines boredom in The Pleasure of the Text. It is often considered a waste of time, but there is nothing to be ashamed of in it. There Barthes distinguishes two experiences: "pleasure" — cozy, familiar, confirming who you are — and "bliss" (in French jouissance) — a jolt that knocks out your usual bearings. Hence his paradox: what seems boring sometimes simply hasn't opened up yet, because it asks for a different kind of attention. Boredom, for Barthes, can be a threshold — a sign that your usual ways of getting pleasure are exhausted and that you are ready for something you don't yet recognize. You don't have to flee from it straight into your news feed. You can linger and see what lies behind it.
boredom.practice: When you get bored, stay with it for two minutes without filling the pause. What did you notice that you wouldn't have noticed in a hurry?

quote.text: Boredom is not far from bliss: it is bliss seen from the shores of pleasure.
quote.author: Roland Barthes

joy.text: Almost all philosophies and ideologies have treated pleasure with suspicion, Barthes notes in The Pleasure of the Text: moralists considered it frivolous, strict intellectuals naive. Joy needs no justification — you can simply accept it, as you would accept a gift. Barthes, one of the few theorists who wrote seriously about pleasure, wanted to restore its dignity. He distinguished calm pleasure from sudden "bliss," which knocks you out of your habitual self. Joy doesn't have to be useful, explainable or "earned." It often comes through small things — a phrase, a taste, a gesture. Let it stay exactly like that: don't immediately turn it into a lesson, a report or an occasion for comparison.
joy.practice: Mark one small joy of today with an action rather than a word: finish your coffee slowly, listen to a song to the end, stand in the sun. No explanation of why it's "important."

love.text: "Atopos" — "without a place": with this Greek word Barthes names the beloved, who can't be classified, reduced to a type, explained. The love and tenderness you feel now are perhaps Barthes's central subject: A Lover's Discourse is written from inside being in love, not from a cold distance. The phrase "I love you," for Barthes, communicates nothing — it is not information but an act, performed anew each time. He describes tenderness as a joy mixed with anxiety: a tender gesture gives, but it also reminds you that it may not be meant for you alone. Barthes doesn't turn love into a diagram and doesn't shame its "sentimentality." He shows that your feeling is unique — and at the same time speaks a language common to all lovers.
love.practice: Try to name the person you love in one word — and notice that no word fits. That is "atopos": smile at this failure.

gratitude.text: In all their life together his mother never once made a "remark" to him — Barthes recalls this gentleness with immense appreciation in Camera Lucida, written after her death. Gratitude is a warm feeling, full of life, that holds an acknowledgment: I was given something, and I noticed it. In his lectures on the Neutral Barthes valued "tact" — attention to fine differences, a refusal to press. Gratitude is perhaps best expressed in a precise detail, not in general words. "Thank you for everything" says less than "thank you for the way you kept quiet that time." Gratitude, like the punctum, lives in the particular and the concrete.
gratitude.practice: Thank one person out loud today — not "for everything," but for one very specific small thing: "thank you for the way you…"

hope.text: "Am I in love? — Yes, since I'm waiting," Barthes writes in A Lover's Discourse. Hope, even a quiet one, works in a similar way: it holds a trust in the future that no one guarantees. There Barthes describes the figure "Waiting" in detail: time stretches, every minute fills with imagined scenarios, and the person seems to become waiting itself. Barthes doesn't mock this state; he sees in it a sign of attachment: we wait only for what is precious to us. Hope is a form of waiting, and there's no need to be ashamed of it as "naive." Waiting can be lived, not only endured: you can notice what it tells you about your desires. Hope shows that an openness toward another and toward the future is still alive in you.
hope.practice: Look out the window at something that changes slowly — a cloud, the light, people at a bus stop. Spend a minute waiting without impatience and ask yourself what exactly you are waiting for.

quote.text: Am I in love? — Yes, since I'm waiting.
quote.author: Roland Barthes

nostalgia.text: "That-has-been" — this is how Barthes, in Camera Lucida, formulates the essence of photography: a picture irrefutably testifies that a moment really existed and that it has already passed. Nostalgia is a sweet and bitter longing for what was and won't come again, and Barthes understood it deeply. Hence the aching power of old photographs. In Roland Barthes by Roland Barthes he tenderly examines pictures from his childhood and writes down "anamneses" — short flashes of memory, with no conclusions and no embellishment. Nostalgia, for Barthes, need not be driven away, nor turned into a myth of a "golden age." It is an acknowledgment: what was, really was — and therefore has value.
nostalgia.practice: Take one old photograph and find a detail in it that says "that-has-been": a button, a shadow, a shop sign. Look at it for a minute, without the thought "things were better then."

craving.text: In France, Barthes noted in Mythologies, wine is a "totem-drink": drinking it means belonging, being normal and sociable, while refusing it almost requires an explanation, as if you had broken a rule. A craving — a sharp "I want it right now" — can sweep over you like a wave, and there's nothing shameful in it. Barthes shows that behind this "naturalness" there is a myth — a cultural script passed off as nature, concealing a lot that is inconvenient, economics included. A craving is not only a bodily impulse but also a script: "after work you're supposed to," "this is how people unwind," "I'll just check in case I missed something." Noticing someone else's borrowed script in your craving gives you a little distance while the wave rises and subsides.
craving.practice: When the craving comes, take a few slow breaths out, and with each one say silently: "This is a script, not me." Listen for whose voice it is, and wait while the wave shifts.

addiction.text: Who sets the rhythm of your day? Barthes built his lecture course How to Live Together (1976–1977) around this question and introduced the word "idiorrhythmy" — from the Greek for "one's own rhythm." Addiction — a long-running loop in which your whole life adjusts to a single rhythm — is not a moral failure. Barthes took the word from the monks of Mount Athos, who lived side by side but each in his own rhythm. Barthes was looking for a form of life in which a person neither dissolves into someone else's rigid routine nor is left completely alone. In this light, addiction is a rhythm imposed by a single object: it decides when to get up, where to go, whom to see. The way out is not a heroic leap but a gradual return of your own rhythm, often alongside others who are looking for the same.
addiction.practice: Do one thing today "in your own rhythm" — take a walk, cook a meal, call someone — not on craving's schedule. If you'd like, find a mutual-help group: there each person lives in their own rhythm, but not alone.

hangover.text: Barthes wrote a whole book about himself in the third person — Roland Barthes by Roland Barthes — as if looking at himself from a little way off, with irony and tenderness. The morning after brings heaviness, anxiety, shame, gaps in memory — and you deserve gentleness. In that book he writes a lot about the "image-repertoire" (the imaginary) — the stock of images we build of ourselves and that, it seems to us, others see in us. The "moral hangover" can be described in his language: in the morning the image-repertoire shows the worst footage — I was ridiculous, I ruined everything, everyone saw. Images of shame are not the whole truth about you but a montage spliced together by anxiety. You can notice them as frames without accepting them as a verdict.
hangover.practice: Tell yourself last night in the third person, in two or three calm sentences, like a chronicler: "He came, talked, left." Then rest a hand on your belly and take a few slow breaths.

euphoria.text: "The text of pleasure: the text that contents, fills, grants euphoria," Barthes writes in The Pleasure of the Text, and he sets pleasure (plaisir) apart from bliss. The high you are in now, when everything seems possible, is a real and vivid experience, and you can truly treasure it. "Bliss" (jouissance) is sharper, almost dizzying: it knocks you out of the familiar and unsettles you. Barthes doesn't rank one above the other or moralize. He only notes that bliss is hard to put into words — it slips away from language. Euphoria doesn't need to be explained or immediately put to use. You can simply live it, and then carefully find a few words of your own for it.
euphoria.practice: Find three words of your own for this high — not borrowed, not from advertising — and say them aloud, like the title of a fragment. That way the moment keeps a voice.

crash.text: Rapture, waiting, anxiety, despondency — in A Lover's Discourse Barthes deliberately arranged the figures in alphabetical order rather than in the order of a plot. A sharp drop after a high — a celebration, a success, a substance — can feel like a fall, as if everything good had been a trick; but that is not the truth about you. Barthes explained that he didn't want to build a story with a setup, a climax and an inevitable collapse: the figures come and go in any order. The drop is one of the figures, not the last chapter. An anxious mind immediately composes a plot: "here comes the payback, it will only get worse from here." But life doesn't have to follow that script, and the joy that was there does not become unreal because of the drop.
crash.practice: Name your state as a "figure" — one word with a capital letter: "Comedown," "The Quiet After." Notice: it is a fragment, not the whole novel.

panic.text: Writing Degree Zero — this is what Barthes called his early book about a "blank," neutral writing that refuses dramatic effects and simply records what is happening. A wave of terror, a pounding heart, the thought "I'm about to die or go mad" — this is one of the most frightening experiences, and you really are scared. Barthes didn't write about panic directly, but, extending his thought, panic speaks the language of catastrophe: it instantly turns every sensation into a tragic plot. The counterweight is to shift to "degree zero": to name things simply, without continuing the story. A wave of panic usually peaks and subsides within a few minutes; simple words help you wait it out.
panic.practice: Put your feet on the floor and breathe out longer than you breathe in. Name out loud what you see in "zero-degree" words: "table. window. blue mug."

dread.text: "He is dead and he is going to die": Barthes sees both at once in a photo of a young man about to be executed. Existential dread — "what is all this for," finitude, the abyss — is a heavy feeling, and Barthes knew it: he wrote Camera Lucida after his mother's death. He calls the most piercing thing in a photograph the "punctum" — the detail that wounds you in particular — and notes that old pictures also prick us with time itself: everything in them has already passed. But Barthes draws from this a conclusion not about meaninglessness but about love: he searched among the photographs for one in which his mother would be recognizable as unique — and found it, a childhood photograph in the Winter Garden. So finitude makes every being irreplaceable. The abyss is the other side of the fact that every life, including yours, is singular and precious.
dread.practice: Find one photograph — of yourself or someone close — and linger on a detail that moves you. Say aloud what makes this person unique.

fomo.text: A guidebook decides in advance what is "worth seeing" — monuments, views — and makes the people and the ordinary life of a country invisible: this is how Barthes, in Mythologies, read the popular "Blue Guide." The feeling that life is happening somewhere else, to other people, really does gnaw, especially in the evening with a phone in your hand. "Myth," for Barthes, is a cultural convention passed off as the natural order of things. A social media feed is a huge guidebook: it decides which life is "worth it" and passes off selected frames as the norm. Noticing this means reclaiming your right to the unremarkable moments, marked in no guide, that your life is actually made of.
fomo.practice: Step outside for five minutes and find a "non-sight" — a place or moment that appears in no guidebook and no feed. Look at it as if it were the city's main monument.

sleepless.text: Dis-cursus — in Latin, "running to and fro," "dashing about": this is how Barthes, in the preface to A Lover's Discourse, explains the very word "discourse." Thoughts at three in the morning dash about too — they spin, come back, won't let you sleep — and it is exhausting. That's how Barthes describes the lover's speech, which dashes from one scene to another. Night thoughts are the same running to and fro: not reasoning that leads to a conclusion, but fragments that surface on their own. Barthes didn't demand that fragments add up to a system. At night you don't need to resolve every question or think every thought through to the end: you can recognize that this is discursus, dashing about, and not the truth about your life.
sleepless.practice: Say to yourself: "This is discursus, dashing about," — and answer each fragment that surfaces not with a thought but with a slow breath out. In the morning the fragments may look different.

betrayal.text: As if you had suddenly glimpsed the underside — this is how Barthes describes the figure "Alteration" (altération), when the image of the beloved, whole and bright until now, is spoiled by a single word, gesture or detail. When you are betrayed, the image of someone you trusted collapses, and your pain is legitimate. Barthes does not shame the one who trusted: he shows that every lover knows this blow. In betrayal what collapses is not only your bond with the person but also the image you had carefully built. It is a double loss, and you may grieve each one separately. And the fact that you trusted this image speaks of your capacity to love and to see the good, not of foolishness.
betrayal.practice: Say two short sentences aloud: "I am losing a person…" and "I am losing an image…". Allow yourself to grieve each one separately.

jealousy.text: Four wounds at once — from the jealousy itself, from reproaching yourself for it, from the fear of hurting the other, and from the sense of having given in to something banal: this is how Barthes, in A Lover's Discourse, describes the jealous person's suffering. If jealousy torments you and embarrasses you on top of that, you are in good company: Barthes writes about it with rare honesty. Most of the torment, then, is not the jealousy itself but the layers of shame and self-condemnation around it. Barthes doesn't shame the jealous person or treat them — he shows that this is a common, recognizable "figure" that lovers pass through, both in books and in life. Recognizing it already removes a layer or two of suffering.
jealousy.practice: Break your jealousy down into layers: "I'm jealous," "I scold myself for it," "I'm afraid of hurting them," "I'm ashamed." Which layer could you let go of first?

quote.text: As a jealous man, I suffer four times over: because I am jealous, because I blame myself for being so, because I fear that my jealousy will wound the other, because I allow myself to be subject to a banality.
quote.author: Roland Barthes

resentment.text: There is an answer to every last word — which is why a scene, Barthes notes, can in principle go on forever. An old resentment carried for years is heavy: it replays the old scene again and again. A Lover's Discourse contains the figure "Scene" — a quarrel in which each wants the last word to be theirs. An old resentment is a scene that continues inside you: you are still looking for that one line that will set everything right. Your resentment speaks of a real wound, and Barthes doesn't demand that you "let it go." But you can notice: there is no last word, and your dignity doesn't depend on whether it is ever spoken.
resentment.practice: Write down that "last line" you still keep saying in your head — and fold the paper in half. Let it be spoken, at least on paper.

heartbreak.text: The other leaves, and I remain — and the discourse of absence, Barthes notes, is always carried on by the one who stays. A broken heart hurts almost physically; it is one of the most human of wounds: the person has gone, but the speech to them goes on. The lover endlessly addresses the one who has gone, "talks" with them in their head, and Barthes doesn't consider this weakness or foolishness. He describes it as an ancient, shared form of the lover's speech, familiar to the heroes of novels and to everyone who has loved. Your inner speech to the one who left is not an obsession but the work of a love that still needs to speak itself out. In time this speech will grow quieter on its own.
heartbreak.practice: Say aloud, alone, what keeps circling inside you — a few sentences to the one who left, with no address and no reply. Let the speech say itself out.

impostor.text: "It must all be considered as if spoken by a character in a novel" — with this inscription Barthes opens Roland Barthes by Roland Barthes. The fear of being exposed any minute often torments precisely those who can do more than they think. There Barthes writes about himself in the third person, in fragments, and shows that the "I" is not a fixed essence that can be caught and exposed, but a changeable image assembled from roles, languages and other people's words. "Impostor syndrome" stems from a myth of the "real expert" that others supposedly are from within, by nature. But everyone plays roles they once learned. This is not deception — it's how any professional life works.
impostor.practice: Tell yourself aloud about yourself at work in the third person, like a character: "She is learning…, knows how to…, doesn't yet know…" Notice that the character changes — as it should.

quote.text: It must all be considered as if spoken by a character in a novel.
quote.author: Roland Barthes
quote.source: Roland Barthes by Roland Barthes (1975), epigraph

self_hatred.text: Wine, steak, Garbo's face — in Mythologies Barthes showed how the most ordinary things acquire a myth that turns history into nature: what came about by chance and by someone's will begins to sound like an eternal "that's how it is." Self-hatred and the voice of the inner critic are exhausting, and that voice does not tell the truth about you. The inner critic speaks precisely the language of myth: "you're like that," "you always," "you never." These phrases pass themselves off as a description of your nature, though they were put together from other people's words, judgments and stories. Barthes called the common opinion that seems self-evident "doxa," and all his life he resisted its power. The critic is your personal doxa. You don't have to refute it; you can see in it what Barthes saw: a constructed phrase, not the truth.
self_hatred.practice: Say one of the critic's phrases out loud and add at the end: "…says the myth." Ask where this phrase came into your life from: this is history, not nature.

helplessness.text: Neither yes nor no, neither victory nor defeat — in his lecture course The Neutral (1977–1978) Barthes looked for what evades an imposed choice between two options. Helplessness — the sense that nothing depends on you — is heavy and often reflects real circumstances. The neutral for him is neither indifference nor weakness but a special, quiet form of strength: a refusal of pressure, of obligatory victory, of "all or nothing." Helplessness is often born of a rigid pair: either I change everything, or I'm powerless. The neutral offers a third way: not to battle with what is beyond your power, while remaining attentive, gentle and alive — toward yourself and others. That too is a way of being present.
helplessness.practice: Instead of "all or nothing," name one "neutral" action: one that doesn't solve the problem but is kind — tea, a call, a walk.

procrastination.text: Barthes devoted the last two years of his lectures at the Collège de France to a novel he never wrote: in the course The Preparation of the Novel, which later became an important book, he examined, in detail, honestly and with humor, the very wish to write — the dream, the doubts, the daily routine, the notes. If you just can't get started, it is exhausting, and laziness has nothing to do with it. Barthes showed that the wish to write is already part of the work, and that a long preparation lies between an idea and the first word. Procrastination often feeds on a fantasy of a too-perfect result. Sometimes it helps to do what Barthes did: notes, fragments, "preparation" — without demanding a finished whole from yourself.
procrastination.practice: Don't start the task — "prepare" it: five minutes of notes, fragments, questions, with no obligation that a whole will come out of it right away.

uprooted.text: The murmur of an unknown language, Barthes wrote of Japan, whose language he didn't understand, envelops the traveler like a protective membrane. Being cut off from home — emigration, a move, the loss of familiar ground — is a real loss of language, people, familiar small things. But in Empire of Signs he finds in the foreign language not only disorientation but also rest — freedom from the endless stream of meanings that at home press in from all sides. Barthes didn't deny the difficulties — he suggested noticing something else too: in a foreign language you are for a while free of doxa, of the ready-made opinions of your own milieu. Uprootedness is both a loss and a strange freedom to see everything anew.
uprooted.practice: Walk for about five minutes and listen to the speech around you like music, without trying to understand: let it be a membrane. Then silently say one word of your native language that you want to keep.

overload.text: To see a photograph well, it is sometimes best to close your eyes, Barthes wrote in Camera Lucida. The feed, the noise, the endless messages wear out a great many people, and it is not your weakness: the stream simply knows no pause. In Camera Lucida Barthes distinguished two levels in a photograph. The "studium" is general interest: we politely examine a picture and take in information. The "punctum" is a detail that suddenly "pricks" you in particular. The feed is an endless studium: everything is moderately interesting, nothing touches you. That's what makes you tired. Relief comes not from one more scroll but from a pause in which you can notice your punctum — the few things that truly concern you.
overload.practice: Close the feed and your eyes for a minute. What one thing you saw today did "prick" you after all? The rest you can let go.

unreality.text: In Flaubert's "A Simple Heart" a barometer is mentioned that means nothing for the plot — and in his essay "The Reality Effect" (1968) Barthes asks: why is it there? The sense that everything around you, or you yourself, is somehow not quite real can be strange and unsettling, and it deserves gentle care. Barthes answers: such useless details are exactly what create the sense of reality — they say "this really exists." In moments of unreality the world seems to lose precisely these small, insignificant details. And you can return to the sense of the real by the same path — through the most ordinary things: a scratch on the table, the hum of the fridge, the weight of keys in your hand.
unreality.practice: Find three "barometers" around you — utterly insignificant details: a scratch, a hum, keys — and name each one aloud. They are what say: "this really exists."

awe.text: The Eiffel Tower, Barthes noticed in a 1964 essay, is both an object looked at from all over Paris and a place from which the whole city is looked at. Awe before something vast or beautiful is a rare, precious feeling, and you can simply enjoy it. From its height Paris becomes a panorama: familiar streets suddenly come together into a whole that can't be seen from below. Barthes describes this as a special pleasure — seeing and understanding at the same time. Awe is perhaps a shift from your usual point of view to a panoramic one: your world suddenly turns out to be larger than you thought, and you a part of it. It doesn't need explaining — you can simply stay at this height for a while.
awe.practice: Go to the highest window you can reach, or simply lift your gaze above the rooftops. For a minute, watch the familiar world come together into a panorama.

relief.text: The lover waits for a call, a whole play is already running in their head — anxiety, reproaches, catastrophes — and then the other walks in, and the whole theater falls apart: this is how Barthes describes the end of waiting. Relief — when things let go and you can breathe out — is worth noticing and living through. Barthes knew this theater from the inside and described it with humor: so much drama — all for a minute that never came. Relief is the moment when the play of the imagination ends and reality begins, usually far simpler. There's a gentle lesson in this too: many scenes we lived through in tension were never actually performed. Relief needs no justification — you can simply breathe with it.
relief.practice: Recall one "scene" you replayed in tension that never actually happened. Take three slow breaths out — one for each of its acts.

calm.text: Silence, tact, delicacy, stepping aside, sleep — in his lectures on the Neutral (1978), Barthes tenderly listed things rarely valued in a world that demands you constantly take a position, argue, win. The calm you are in now is neither emptiness nor inaction, and it is good simply to be in it, without hurrying anywhere. The "Neutral" for him is a desire to step out for a while from the battle of meanings, from the duty to have an opinion about everything. He stressed that this is not indifference but a subtle, living sensitivity. Calm is the Neutral lived through the body: a moment when you are proving nothing to anyone. It doesn't need to be justified by productivity.
calm.practice: Sit for a minute without forming an opinion about anything. If an opinion appears, just label it "opinion" — and return to the quiet.

inspiration.text: A text is a fabric woven of quotations, references, echoes, Barthes wrote — and the Latin textus itself means "woven." When thoughts and images suddenly start connecting, it is one of the most joyful states. In "The Death of the Author" Barthes argues against the image of the lone genius from whom everything springs "from within." A text, for Barthes, is woven from many other voices, quotations, cultural echoes; the writer doesn't create from nothing but combines, mixes, interweaves. This is not a belittling but a liberation: inspiration doesn't have to arise from a void. Inspiration is the moment when many things you've read, heard and seen suddenly begin talking to each other through you. There's no need to fear that it's "not yours": your unrepeatable pattern lies in the weaving itself.
inspiration.practice: Write down the idea that came, and next to it three voices it may be woven from: a book, a conversation, a place.

quote.text: The text is a tissue of quotations drawn from the innumerable centres of culture.
quote.author: Roland Barthes

schadenfreude.text: The wrestling crowd exults when the "bastard" in the ring finally gets beaten, and Barthes noted in Mythologies that spectators come not for sport but for the spectacle of Justice: they need to see villainy get what it deserves. A sudden joy at someone else's failure is familiar to everyone and says little about what kind of person you are. Schadenfreude is often built the same way: for a moment you look at life as a ring where the upstart, the offender or the "too lucky" one gets what's coming. It is an understandable thirst for simple justice in a world where there's so little of it. But life isn't wrestling, and the "villain" almost always has a story of their own that can't be seen from the stands.
schadenfreude.practice: Ask yourself: "In what show is this person playing the villain for me?" Recall what injustice toward yourself you felt at that moment — and simply name it.

contempt.text: The petty bourgeois is unable to imagine the Other, Barthes wrote in "Myth Today": if the Other does appear, he is either ignored or remade into a likeness of oneself. Contempt seems calm and confident, but behind it there often hides a fear of the unlike. In the same essay Barthes describes the rhetorical devices by which "myth" defends itself against the other. He calls one of them "identification." Another device is "exoticism": the stranger is turned into an amusing curiosity, a clown, an object. Contempt is one such way of not truly meeting another person: they have been put in a labeled box in advance. The feeling may have a real cause, and there's no need to be ashamed of it. But it helps to notice the moment when a living person turns into a "type" for you — and for a second give them back their face.
contempt.practice: Silently describe this person without evaluative words — only through actions and facts, like a chronicler. Notice the moment when the "type" becomes a face again.

disgust.text: Barthes felt almost physically nauseous at "doxa" — ready-made public opinion, the stereotype, the phrase repeated a thousand times. Disgust is a sharp, bodily "no," and there's nothing shameful in it: this is how body and soul mark a boundary. Barthes learned to recognize this feeling and to ask what exactly it was reacting to. Disgust at people, a situation or yourself is often directed not at a living person but at a frozen image: the stereotype of "people like that," a scene that sets your teeth on edge, other people's words about you. Disgust honestly points to what you find unbearable. But it's worth checking whom it concerns — the person, or the cliché that they, or you, turned into for a moment.
disgust.practice: Notice where in your body the disgust lives, and breathe out slowly. Then ask silently: "Is it the person that disgusts me — or the cliché that they (or I) turned into for a moment?"

revenge.text: Blow or counterblow, yes or no — Barthes called such a rigid pair a "paradigm," and in his lectures on the Neutral he looked for a way out of it. You were hurt, and the hurt demands an outlet; there's no need to deny it. He understood the Neutral not as limpness but as a subtle art of stepping out of this forced pair. Revenge is a classic paradigm: "he struck — I must answer," and the choice seems reduced to two squares. But there are third moves too: stepping back, naming your pain, refusing to play by imposed rules. Refusing revenge then is not capitulation but your freedom not to be locked into someone else's script.
revenge.practice: Walk for a few minutes and, as you go, come up with a third move — neither blow nor counterblow: stepping back, naming your pain, refusing to play by imposed rules.

quote.text: I call Neutral everything that baffles the paradigm.
quote.author: Roland Barthes
quote.source: The Neutral, lecture course at the Collège de France (1977–1978)

anger_at_loved.text: "This can't go on" — with this sentence the figure "The Unbearable" bursts out in Barthes: small hurts and things left unsaid pile up unnoticed until one day they break through. Anger at someone close often flares more strongly than at strangers, and afterward you feel ashamed; that doesn't mean you love badly. Barthes shows that this explosion is not a sudden change of heart but the result of a long, silent accumulation. A flash of anger at someone close often speaks not of today's trifle but of many unspoken "trifles" before it. Anger doesn't give you the right to wound, but it does give you a reason to notice what has long been asking to be said — more calmly, and sooner than the next explosion.
anger_at_loved.practice: Choose one of the small things that built up before the flare-up and mention it to your loved one calmly, at a good moment, in one sentence.

ambivalence.text: A rude word, a foreign intonation, a gesture — and through the ideal image of the beloved someone else shows through: in A Lover's Discourse Barthes describes how the image cracks. Loving someone and not being able to stand them at the same time is a hard, confusing, but very common state. Barthes doesn't conclude from this that the love was a mistake. The crack shows that before you is not a picture but a living person who doesn't coincide with your image of them. Mixed feelings are the price of meeting a real other rather than an ideal. "I can't stand" and "I love" can refer to the same person, because they are larger than any picture you have of them.
ambivalence.practice: Recall the last moment of "cracking" and put your hand where it echoed in your body. Ask yourself: what broke — the person themselves, or my image of them?

guilty_relief.text: Barthes's mother was ill for a long time, he cared for her, and after her death he kept notes later published as Mourning Diary: grief in them comes in waves, and between the waves there is work, ordinary life, even lightness. Relief after the death of a gravely ill loved one, a breakup or long caregiving can be frightening, but relief and love can live side by side. Barthes doesn't arrange these states into a "proper" scheme and doesn't discard those that seem unseemly. Relief is one of these unevennesses, not a confession of not loving. Long caregiving and long anxiety come to an end, and the body breathes out. That exhale doesn't cancel the love that was there and remains.
guilty_relief.practice: Write on a card, as Barthes did, one honest sentence about your relief — and one about what you continue to love or value.

indifference.text: The punctum can't be summoned on demand, Barthes insisted: it either happens or it doesn't. Sometimes what "should" move you leaves you indifferent — and guilt follows. In Camera Lucida Barthes distinguishes two ways of looking at a photograph. The "studium" is a polite, general interest: we understand that the picture is important and acknowledge its significance, but it doesn't wound us. The "punctum" is a detail that suddenly "pricks" you in particular, often unexpected and unrelated to what "should" stir you. Indifference where you're "supposed" to be moved is simply a state of studium. It is not proof of your callousness. Response comes by its own paths and in its own time; sometimes you'll be touched by something entirely different from what was prescribed — and that is honest too.
indifference.practice: For five minutes, demand no feeling of yourself: just look around and wait to see whether something "pricks" on its own — a sound, a light, a small thing. If nothing does, that is honest too.

escape.text: Reading Jacques Lacarrière's book about Greece, Barthes came across the word "idiorrhythmy": on Mount Athos there were monasteries where each monk lived in his own rhythm while remaining part of the community. His course How to Live Together begins with this dream. The wish to drop everything and leave — a job, a city, a role — says that life has become cramped, and it is an important signal. Barthes honestly called his dream a fantasy, but believed the fantasy was worth exploring: it points to a real need. The dream of escape often says not "vanish from here" but "live in my own rhythm." Perhaps the point is not to drop everything but to reclaim a little of your own rhythm right where you are.
escape.practice: Choose one small thing from a day "in your own rhythm" — an unhurried breakfast, the walk on foot, an hour without calls — and arrange it for yourself this week. This is your little Athos.

forbidden_attraction.text: Werther sees Charlotte for the first time as she cuts bread for the children — and that image is enough: Barthes calls such a moment the figure "Ravishment," a capture. Attraction to someone unavailable or "wrong" can be confusing and frightening, but a feeling in itself is not an action. Barthes shows that capture often happens because of a detail, a scene, rather than the whole person. A forbidden attraction is a strong reaction to an image in which you recognized something you very much need. It is neither a verdict nor a command. You can look with curiosity at the scene that captured you and ask what it's telling you.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Picture the "scene" that captured you as a frame from a film: where, what gesture, what light. What in this frame is missing from your own life right now?

social_anxiety.text: The moment Barthes feels a lens on him, he begins to "pose," involuntarily turning into an image — he admits this in Camera Lucida. Fear of people and their judgment is exhausting: as if you're always on stage and everyone is watching. Barthes feels several "I"s colliding in him: the one he thinks he is, the one he wants to appear to be, the one the photographer sees. Barthes describes this without shame, with irony — as a discomfort common to everyone. Social anxiety is a constant sense of the lens: in every encounter you see yourself from outside. It helps to know that almost everyone feels this tension: others are busy with their own poses too. You can gently move your attention from how you look to the person you're talking with.
social_anxiety.practice: In your next conversation, notice one detail about the other person: the color of their eyes, their intonation, a gesture. This brings your attention back from the "lens" to the encounter.

quote.text: In front of the lens, I am at the same time: the one I think I am, the one I want others to think I am, the one the photographer thinks I am, and the one he makes use of to exhibit his art.
quote.author: Roland Barthes

uncertainty.text: Do you know the ending of your own story? In S/Z Barthes distinguished texts whose ending is known in advance from texts that the reader helps write. Uncertainty is hard: it's unclear how things will end, and the mind dashes between options. The "readerly" text is familiar, with a clear plot, where the reader only consumes a ready-made meaning. The "writerly" text is open: it holds many meanings, and the reader takes part in creating them. Barthes considered the second kind more alive, even though it demands more effort. In a period of uncertainty your life becomes a "writerly" text: the ending isn't written in advance, and you take part in creating it. That's unsettling, but there's freedom in it too. You don't need to know the whole plot to write the next paragraph.
uncertainty.practice: Write two or three lines of the "next paragraph" of your story for the coming week — only what depends on you.

waiting.text: "Maybe he's late because…" — so begins the first act of the little theater Barthes describes in A Lover's Discourse. Waiting for an answer, results or news stretches time out, and it's hard to live in. The play has several acts: first, calculations and guesses, then irritation and reproaches, then anxiety and a sense of abandonment. All of it is staged inside while outwardly nothing happens. Barthes shows that this play is put on by the waiting itself, not by real events. Once you recognize the acts of this play, you gain a little more freedom: you can notice "we're in the second act now" and not take every line of the inner play for the truth about the world. The waiting remains, but it becomes a little less commanding.
waiting.practice: Work out which "act" of waiting you're in now: calculations, irritation or anxiety. Name it out loud — and take three slow exhales.

regret.text: "Midway upon the journey of our life" — with this line of Dante, in the 1978 lecture "Longtemps, je me suis couché de bonne heure," Barthes speaks of the "middle of life." Regret over something done or undone can return for years: "if only back then…" Barthes describes the moment when a person suddenly realizes that time is limited and something needs to change. Barthes calls his dream "Vita Nova" — "new life": not a renunciation of the past but a decision to use the remaining time in a new way. Regret is the painful awareness that time is finite and that the choice mattered. But it can also become the start of a "new life": not correcting the past, but paying attention to what you want to do now.
regret.practice: Say aloud in one sentence what you regret, and right after it a second one: "My 'new life' on this could begin with…" Let the second sentence sound louder.

longing.text: In every photograph after his mother's death Barthes saw a woman who looked like her, but not her — and only in one picture, where she stands as a child in a winter garden, did he suddenly recognize her kindness, her particular essence. Longing for a particular person is especially sharp because they can't be replaced. He chose not to publish this picture: it matters only to him, and no one else would see the same in it. Longing is always directed at something singular — not at "a good person in general" but at what exists only in them. Your longing is a sign of this singularity, and it doesn't need to be replaced by consolations like "you'll find someone else."
longing.practice: Recall a detail in which this person is "all there": an intonation, a gesture, a habit. Repeat it yourself — as a gesture or a word, quietly, just for yourself.

world_pain.text: A photographer who tries too hard to shock seems to have screamed for us, and all we can do is agree — this is how Barthes, in Mythologies, explained why "shock-photos" often fail to move us. Pain for the world — from grim news, wars, injustice — can crush you, and it speaks of your capacity for compassion. More restrained pictures, with a simple detail, leave room for our own feeling and thought. A stream of shocking images doesn't make us more compassionate — it deafens us. Pain for the world can be carried more gently if you give yourself not an avalanche of pictures but time to respond: to pause on one story, one face, one cause where your involvement is possible.
world_pain.practice: Choose one news story and switch off the rest of the stream. Ask yourself: what small response — a thought, a word, help — can I offer in return?

rejection.text: "The image excludes me," Barthes writes in A Lover's Discourse: in love, the deepest wounds come not from what we know but from what we see. Rejection wounds painfully, and this pain is real. We see a scene in which we are absent: the other laughing with someone, living a life that has no place for us. This image is incredibly powerful: it seems to declare once and for all that you are excluded. The pain of rejection is largely sustained by such images — they replay again and again before the inner eye. But an image is not yet the whole truth about you and your worth. You can notice that you're watching a "movie" in which you've been cast as the outcast, and remind yourself that outside this frame you have a life of your own.
rejection.practice: Name the image that comes back to you most often. Then name a scene from your life where, on the contrary, you are a welcome participant.

abandonment.text: A call, an intonation, a delay — Barthes's lover depends entirely on small things, and this dependency seems humiliating to them. The fear of being abandoned is exhausting: you catch every sign, every pause before a reply, and this fear often grows from old wounds. But Barthes describes such dependency without mockery, as part of human love, common to many. He shows that the more the other means to us, the more vulnerable we are to their absence. The fear of abandonment is the other side of deep attachment. That doesn't make the fear any more pleasant, but it lets you not despise yourself for it. It helps to remind yourself that each pause is a pause, not a verdict.
abandonment.practice: When a pause before a reply frightens you, name aloud three harmless reasons for it — and do something nice for yourself without waiting for the reply.

unrequited.text: "Non-will-to-possess" — Barthes borrows this image from Taoism and makes it one of the lover's figures. Unrequited love wounds: a feeling with no answer seems superfluous, in vain. It is not a renunciation of love but a special state of it: to go on loving while ceasing to demand, hold on, pursue. Barthes admits this is hard and almost impossible, but he sees in this movement a gentle release — both for yourself and for the other. Unrequited love can become not only a wound but also an experience of "not grasping": loving while letting the other be free. This is not an obligation but a possibility, one that sometimes brings quiet where there was constant strain.
unrequited.practice: Say to yourself: "I feel what I feel, and I let go of the need to get an answer." Notice what happens in your body as you say it.

humiliation.text: Arrogance, for Barthes, is a manner of speaking that leaves the other no room: it talks down, knows everything, delivers final judgments. Humiliation is one of the most painful experiences: you want the ground to swallow you, to forget the scene. In his lectures on the Neutral Barthes sets delicacy and tact against arrogance. In humiliation you came up against another person's arrogance: their speech tried to make you small, leaving you no voice. But arrogance says more about the speaker than about the one it's aimed at. A humiliating scene doesn't define your worth. You can refuse to accept someone else's verdict as your own and answer yourself with the tact you weren't given.
humiliation.practice: Imagine how a tactful person who respects you would speak about what happened — and say their words aloud, to yourself.

body_shame.text: A mask and an event — this is how Barthes, in the essay "The Face of Garbo," tells apart two famous film faces. Dissatisfaction with your body can be quiet and constant, and it deserves gentleness. Greta Garbo's face, he says, is an "Idea": a flawless, almost abstract mask of beauty. Audrey Hepburn's face is an "Event": alive, unrepeatable, particular. Barthes doesn't say one is better than the other, but he shows how culture creates ideal standards that no living person can coincide with. Your body is not a failed Idea but an Event: it has its own history, its own features, its own way of being in the world. Comparing an event with an abstraction is unfair. You can see yourself as an unrepeatable event rather than a failed copy.
body_shame.practice: Look in a mirror at one feature that makes you recognizable — an "event," not an "idea." Name it aloud with one kind word.

illness.text: Barthes spent several years of his youth in sanatoriums because of tuberculosis — there he read a great deal and wrote his first texts. When the body lets you down, the world narrows: you have to cancel plans and live by someone else's rhythm of treatment and restrictions. Later, in the course How to Live Together, he recalled the sanatorium in Thomas Mann's novel The Magic Mountain and reflected on "idiorrhythmy" — the possibility of living in your own rhythm even amid shared rules. Illness imposes its rhythm, but within it small islands of your own still remain: a morning hour, a book, a thought, a conversation. You can protect them. This doesn't replace health, but it gives back a little of yourself on days when the body has so much say.
illness.practice: Find one "idiorrhythmic" island in your day — an activity entirely in your own rhythm, even for five minutes. Mark it in your calendar.

pride.text: "Biographeme" — Barthes coined the word in the preface to Sade, Fourier, Loyola, dreaming that someday a friendly biographer might reduce his life not to big facts but to a few beloved small things: tastes, gestures, details. Pride in what you've done is a healthy, well-earned feeling worth living through without embarrassment and without looking over your shoulder. Pride is also attention to the biographeme: not only to the result, but to the detail that makes what you did distinctly yours. Maybe it's a decision you made at a difficult moment, or a small touch that no one noticed but you. Pride grows warmer when you see that detail.
pride.practice: Tell someone one small detail of what you did that especially delights you — not the result, but a touch. That is your biographeme.

melancholy.text: Quiet pleasure is no less than upheaval — Barthes insisted on this, defending the right both to calm plaisir and to stormy jouissance. Gentle sadness is a quiet, tender feeling with nothing wrong in it, and it doesn't need fixing. In The Pleasure of the Text Barthes distinguishes two kinds of pleasure: "plaisir" — calm, tied to culture, habit, the coziness of reading — and "jouissance" — bliss that shakes you and throws you off course. Melancholy is a special kind of plaisir: not stormy rapture but a calm, slightly sad enjoyment of an autumn day, an old song, a book you read in your youth. You can savor it like a good text, without demanding that it turn into either joy or grief.
melancholy.practice: Choose one thing that brings you gentle sadness — a song, a place, a book. Give it a few minutes, simply enjoying it.
